brief.head: Accidents of history
brief.text: The world does not set­tle into one equi­lib­rium wher­ever it starts, Ajay Shah said. Little ac­ci­dents deep in the past[[x2]] shape how so­ci­eties, and each of us, un­fold. {003-C03}

brief.head: Mirror, mirror
brief.text: We shape our­selves on how we look in other people’s eyes[[x3]], Amit Varma said. Around Ajay Shah, he would cut out the dad jokes for se­ri­ous econ talk. {003-J05}

brief.head: How to stay hungry
brief.text: In a win­ner-takes-all world, Ajay Shah said, long jour­neys de­mand rare con­cen­tra­tion, or dhyan[[x4]]. Prosaic goals such as mak­ing a lot of money peter out too soon. {003-C11}

brief.head: Peers over parents
brief.text: Amit Varma called Judith Rich Harris’s *The Nurture Assumption* one of the sem­i­nal so­cial sci­ence books of the last cen­tury: peers, not par­ents, shape how chil­dren turn out. {003-R09}

brief.head: Law for everyone
brief.text: India’s legal sys­tem has some 50 el­e­ments need­ing care­ful thought, Ajay Shah said, so all of us must en­gage. “Law is too im­por­tant to be left to the lawyers[[x5]].” {003-J08}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on masks, accusers and soil
lead.head: The mask that becomes the face

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 3

body: Ajay Shah ar­rived clean-shaven. He had read Vladimir Putin’s claim that ev­ery­one sup­ported the in­va­sion of Ukraine ex­cept “some bearded in­tel­lec­tu­als”, and it in­spired him to do some­thing about the beard.
Then he ob­jected. Marx, Engels, Lenin and Trotsky were all bearded, he said: Putin’s own pan­theon “should be full of bearded in­tel­lec­tu­als”. {003-J01}
It was a light start to an episode about get­ting stuck.

Amit Varma began in Jaipur, which he vis­ited in January. Its fa­mous pink­ness, he learnt, dates only from 1876, when the city was painted to com­mem­o­rate a visit by Prince Edward. Tourists now come ex­pect­ing pink, so the fash­ion in the tourist quar­ters is to paint ev­ery­thing pink.

People get frozen the same way, Varma ar­gued. A 14-year-old girl praised at fam­ily gath­er­ings for her smile and her docil­ity learns that pleas­ant­ness wins ap­proval. Boys are pushed to be macho. The per­sona brings val­i­da­tion, and then it be­comes you.
“The mask be­comes a per­son, the per­sona be­comes who you re­ally are,” Varma said. “And that is in­cred­i­bly dan­ger­ous, I think, for peo­ple.” {003-C01}
Audiences tighten the mask. Shah’s ex­am­ple was Fox News, whose view­ers ran away when it told the truth that Trump had lost. The leader, he said, has to stay with the fol­low­ers.
## A cen­tury to rein­vent

What has changed, Shah ar­gued, is time. In the olden days, mean life ex­pectancy at age 20 was about 65, and health de­clined dra­mat­i­cally from about 50. You be­came a com­pany man, or spent 35 years as a civil ser­vant wear­ing one cos­tume.
Today’s 20-year-old, he said, has a hun­dred years to go, time enough to rein­vent one­self many times. “It’s the great­est head­room of all, it’s the great­est lux­ury,” he said. {003-C05}
Varma once balked at the idea of liv­ing to 120: he had watched his fa­ther decay and lose his mem­ory. Now he thinks it may make sense to live as if he had 50 years left, even if he has only 20.
## The power to ac­cuse

In the sec­ond chap­ter, Shah turned to fair play in in­ves­ti­ga­tion and pros­e­cu­tion. India fo­cuses on po­lit­i­cal in­ter­fer­ence, he said, but there is a deeper prob­lem: in­ves­ti­ga­tors fall for a pet the­ory, and con­fir­ma­tion bias does the rest.

His rem­edy comes in lay­ers. A sep­a­rate pub­lic pros­e­cu­tor, judged on win rate, should refuse weak cases. A grand jury of cit­i­zens adds an­other check, though in the UK such ju­ries were too often over­awed by pros­e­cu­tors.

In India, he said, the pic­ture is patchy. The in­come tax de­part­ment and SEBI run on com­plete ex­ec­u­tive dis­cre­tion; the pub­lic pros­e­cu­tor has with­ered; the CBI keeps in­ves­ti­ga­tor and pros­e­cu­tor apart.
Varma asked why any gov­ern­ment would give up such tools. “The process is a pun­ish­ment,” he said. {003-C08}

Shah an­swered with a con­fes­sion. Laws he had helped amend, when the op­por­tu­nity was sky high, were not done well, be­cause econ­o­mists like him lacked knowl­edge of law and pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion.
## Free books, poor leaves
For his rec­om­men­da­tion, Varma urged lis­ten­ers to read Eamonn Butler’s primers on clas­si­cal lib­er­al­ism, Hayek, Mises, Milton Friedman, Adam Smith and pub­lic choice, free on the web­site.
Shah of­fered an anti-recommendation. Hydroponic leaves look pris­tine, he said, but with­out the root mi­cro­biome of healthy soil their nu­tri­tion is sys­tem­at­i­cally in­fe­rior. {003-C12}
The hosts ended at the din­ner table: Tolstoy’s live chicken, the prom­ise of lab-grown meat, and fruit flies that lived shorter lives after merely see­ing dead ones.

second.label: Captured by the audience
second.head: Fox follows its flock
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why a channel carried the stolen-election theories

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Fox News and its fleeing viewers

body: After the US pres­i­den­tial elec­tion, Fox News tried to tell the truth: Trump had lost. Its au­di­ence began to run away, Ajay Shah said, and that threat­ened to be­come a big fi­nan­cial prob­lem. {003-S03}

So the chan­nel car­ried the con­spir­acy the­o­ries about a stolen elec­tion, to hang on to its view­er­ship. Shah’s les­son: the leader has to stay with the fol­low­ers, be­cause if the fol­low­ers are not there, she is not a leader any more.

Amit Varma had made the same point about web­sites known for one point of view, pro-government or anti-government, which must stay true to that char­ac­ter be­cause it brings traf­fic. Online, he said, val­i­da­tion makes peo­ple dou­ble down until “you be­come that per­son”. {003-C02}

quote.text: So it was lit­er­ally a busi­ness de­ci­sion at Fox News to carry the en­tire con­spir­acy the­o­ries around the stolen elec­tion.

third.head: Flies that saw too much

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on fruit flies that saw dead fruit flies

body: Ajay Shah closed the episode with one last story. In re­cent sci­en­tific ex­per­i­ments, fruit flies were ex­posed to noth­ing more than the sight of dead fruit flies. It had an ad­verse im­pact on their life­span. {003-S10}

Amit Varma checked that he had it right: flies that saw dead flies lived shorter lives than those that did not. Shah said hu­mans ob­vi­ously suf­fer a moral in­jury from see­ing death, as on a bat­tle­field, and that it ex­tends to other mam­mals, to birds and all the way down to the fruit fly.
“The mind goes all the way down to flies,” he said.
For Shah, that is rea­son to re­spect all life, and to wel­come ar­ti­fi­cial meat[[x1]]. Both hosts are ex­cited by meat grown in a lab, with­out any an­i­mal ever ex­ist­ing. {003-J12}

box.title: Why Jaipur is pink
box.text: Tourists now ex­pect pink, but Jaipur’s pink­ness is not an­cient, Amit Varma read. He does not know why that colour was cho­sen. In 1876, he said, the city was painted pink to com­mem­o­rate a visit by Prince Edward. {#pink}

sections.label: The first idea
sections.head: Painted pink, stuck pink
sections.caption: the pinkness of Jaipur
body: Amit Varma went to Jaipur in January as a tourist and, be­cause he loves cities, read up on it. The Pink City’s colour, he found, is not old. It was painted pink to com­mem­o­rate a visit by Prince Edward.

Varma does not know why pink. But the label be­came a brand the city had to wear. Tourists ar­rive ex­pect­ing pink, so the fash­ion is to paint ev­ery­thing pink. Even peo­ple who rebel against the pink­ness, he said, end up re­in­forc­ing the idea that this is the pink city. {003-S01}
## Social pro­gram­ming

Ajay Shah agreed that we are all crea­tures of so­cial pro­gram­ming, praised al­most at ran­dom down cer­tain routes. He likened aware­ness of it to an AI that un­der­stands its op­er­at­ing sys­tem: hu­mans, he said, can put their cul­ture under the mi­cro­scope and won­der whether they could be dif­fer­ent. {003-C04}

Varma raised the look­ing-glass self: we shape our­selves on our re­flec­tion in other people’s eyes, so the com­pany we keep mat­ters. Shah was wary of so much cal­cu­la­tion. Life throws us in with peo­ple, he said, and we are blessed if they are good. {003-C06}
~ Varma quoted John Lennon: life is what hap­pens to you when you’re busy mak­ing other plans. Back came the reply: “Or life is what hap­pens to you while you’re busy mak­ing pod­casts.” {003-J06}

quote.text: Jaipur could have been many things, but it be­came a pink city.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the pinkness of Jaipur

sections.label: The second idea
sections.head: A jury before the trial
sections.caption: checks on the power to accuse
body: Political in­ter­fer­ence is not the only thing wrong with in­ves­ti­ga­tion and pros­e­cu­tion in India, Ajay Shah said. Investigators are frail and human: they form a pet the­ory and, through con­fir­ma­tion bias, start see­ing only the facts that sup­port it. {003-C07}

His first layer of de­fence is a sep­a­rate pub­lic pros­e­cu­tor[[x6]], a neu­tral party with a check­list of the el­e­ments a crime re­quires. Three out of four is not enough. Prosecutors judged on their win rate, he said, will be loath to bring friv­o­lous cases. {#winrate}
## The citizens’ veto

The sec­ond layer was in­vented in the UK around the 14th and 15th cen­turies, when peo­ple felt the state had too much dis­cre­tion: a grand jury of cit­i­zens who must agree there is enough to in­dict. It largely faded there, be­cause ju­ries were too often over­awed by pros­e­cu­tors. {003-S05}

Citizens, Shah said, need to be im­bued with pub­lic choice the­ory and scep­ti­cism. And the in­dict­ment of Donald Trump in the US raised a new prob­lem: in a ran­dom sam­ple of peo­ple, some 30 per cent are po­lit­i­cally rad­i­calised. {#radical}
~ Copying the US, the UK or Japan will not work, Shah said. Building the re­pub­lic means many hard prob­lems, each “a twenty year, forty year, sixty year jour­ney”. {003-C09}

quote.text: Once you have a point of view, the en­tire uni­verse or­ga­nizes it­self to give you facts that en­hance and sup­port your be­lief.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on checks on the power to accuse

sections.label: The third idea
sections.head: The patient wants ivermectin
sections.caption: the dharma of a profession
body: Every call­ing has a dharma[[x7]], Amit Varma said. A lawyer serves the client, but within the law. A doc­tor heals. A jour­nal­ist speaks truth to power or, in the old maxim, af­flicts the com­fort­able and com­forts the af­flicted. {003-J09}

Each is pulled the other way by an in­cen­tive to give peo­ple what they de­mand. A doctor’s dharma, Varma said, is to do what is best for the pa­tient; the in­cen­tive is to give the pa­tient what he wants, even the wrong thing. {003-C10}
A jour­nal­ist work­ing for a media or­gan­i­sa­tion may like­wise give the mar­ket one side of a nar­ra­tive bat­tle rather than the truth.
His friend Murali Neelakantan, for many years a law-firm part­ner in the UK and the US, came back to India and took on a client who ex­pected him to lie on his be­half. {003-S07}
## Parents, then courts
Ajay Shah said dharma is shaped first by par­ents, then, as Varma sug­gested with UK courts and per­jury, by in­sti­tu­tions.

~ Echoing their friend Suyash Rai, Shah added that the state is nei­ther nec­es­sary nor suf­fi­cient. Most of our moral code is en­forced be­tween peo­ple, and the state should do only a small part of it.

quote.text: In England per­jury is the ex­cep­tion and it ends a lawyer’s ca­reer if you do it. But in India it is a norm.
quote.who: Murali Neelakantan, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Amit’s pick
sections.head: Free lessons in liberty
sections.caption: Eamonn Butler’s primers
body: People often ask Amit Varma what to read to un­der­stand in­di­vid­ual free­dom, clas­si­cal lib­er­al­ism, or thinkers he ad­mires such as Adam Smith and Hayek. He thinks it a re­ally im­por­tant ques­tion.

Many ideas we pick up by os­mo­sis when young, he said, make us feel in­cred­i­bly vir­tu­ous, as if we were serv­ing so­cial jus­tice. They tend to be ideas of so­cial­ism, which im­plic­itly use the co­er­cive power of the state: deeply il­lib­eral ideas. {003-J10}
## A shelf of primers

His an­swer is a se­ries by Eamonn Butler[[x8]], who works at a think tank in the UK and is, in Varma’s opin­ion, one of the finest lib­eral minds in the world. Butler has primers on clas­si­cal lib­er­al­ism, Hayek, Mises, Milton Friedman, pub­lic choice and Adam Smith. {003-R01}

The pub­lic choice primer he called out­stand­ing, be­cause the books of Buchanan and Tullock can make for com­plex read­ing. So can Hayek’s, “though what a great writer”. Butler, Varma said, gets to the heart of each sub­ject and breaks it down beau­ti­fully.
~ The primers are sold as cheap Kindle books and can also be had free on the web­site. “These books are an ed­u­ca­tion,” Varma said, “and it is a mir­a­cle that they are free.”

quote.text: A lot of the ideas that we pick up by os­mo­sis when we are young are ideas that make us feel in­cred­i­bly vir­tu­ous

sections.label: Ajay’s anti-pick
sections.head: Dirty soil, better salad
sections.caption: the root microbiome
body: Ajay Shah came with no rec­om­men­da­tion, only an anti-recommendation, for some­thing no­body should do: hy­dro­pon­ics, the “lit­tle cult” of grow­ing leaves and veg­eta­bles in water with nu­tri­ents.
Its ap­peal, he said, is su­per­fi­cial. Hydroponic veg­eta­bles are very clean: they do not come from the mess of the soil, they carry no in­sects or worms, and they need less wash­ing.
## What lives below
The in­sight lies in the root mi­cro­biome. The human gut, Shah said[[x9]], holds one to two kilo­grams of bac­te­ria and yeasts that make com­plex chem­i­cals the body uses. {#gut}

In the same way, a plant grow­ing in soil re­lies on a root mi­cro­biome that con­structs com­plex chem­i­cals for it. Kill it with chem­i­cal fer­tilis­ers, pes­ti­cides or ex­ces­sive plough­ing, or grow the plant in water, and its nu­tri­ents are sys­tem­at­i­cally in­fe­rior. {003-C12}

His ad­vice is to favour the mess of soil that has not been ploughed and has not faced chem­i­cal fer­tilis­ers or pes­ti­cides. Amit Varma had a dif­fer­ent ob­jec­tion to leaves. “Anybody who’s eat­ing a leaf, it’s a su­per­fi­cial joy only,” he said. {003-J11}
~ Both hosts are ex­cited by meat grown in a lab. Varma came to it by way of Tolstoy’s chicken on the chair. {003-S09}

quote.text: We should look be­yond the su­per­fi­cial hap­pi­ness that we get out of hav­ing a pris­tine leaf

art.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on the root microbiome, with Amit Varma

quote.text: So all of us are crea­tures are made by so­cial pro­gram­ming. We can’t deny it. We can’t will it away. We can’t wish it away. It is there. Our only choice is to be­come self-aware.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A live chicken, a sweet question, a doctor’s restraint and an economist’s confession

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Tolstoy, his aunt and a dinner invitation
stories.head: The meal that squawked back
body: In the last years of his life, Amit Varma said, Leo Tolstoy was “an in­cred­i­bly self-righteous, virtue sig­nal­ing old man” who lec­tured ev­ery­one: don’t do this, don’t do that, peace and love. One of the things he cared about most was not eat­ing an­i­mals.

One day his aunt, older still, Varma guessed, an­nounced that she was com­ing to din­ner. She wanted chicken, and none of Tolstoy’s talk about veg­e­tar­i­ans. Tolstoy agreed: come, he told her, and you will have chicken.
The aunt duly ar­rived and was taken to the din­ing table. On her chair sat a live chicken[[x10]], going squawk, squawk, squawk. {#squawk}
“You wanted a chicken, there’s your chicken, have it,” Tolstoy told her, in Varma’s telling.

Varma wrote an essay on the story in the late nineties; it is no longer on­line any­where. Under the in­flu­ence of such noble thoughts, when he was some twenty years younger, he turned veg­e­tar­ian for a year, out of com­pas­sion, but could not keep it up. {#veg}
To him the story names a gap we choose to ig­nore. “It’s a seen and the un­seen,” he said. “The chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.” {003-S09}

~ Modern sci­ence may offer a way out, he said: meat grown in a lab, not a meat sub­sti­tute, with­out the an­i­mal ever ex­ist­ing. One could grow a chicken leg or make a steak. We might have our meat and eat it too, “what­ever that might mean”.
stories.why: Lab-grown meat, both hosts hope, might one day close a gap that Tolstoy forced into view: we enjoy the chicken on the plate be­cause we never see the chicken on the chair. {003-C13}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah, too, is ex­cited by lab-grown meat: it would be so nice, he said, to eat meat with­out harm­ing any sen­tient crea­ture.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Tolstoy’s live chicken

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the listener who knew only his show self
stories.head: The man who never shouts?
body: At a book launch a while back, Amit Varma was ap­proached by a cou­ple who had heard every episode of his pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen*. Both were reg­u­lar lis­ten­ers.
The wife asked him, sweetly and sin­cerely, a ques­tion: had he ever shouted at some­one in his life? {003-S02}
Varma felt ter­ri­ble. She knew him only from the show, and had taken its per­sona for the whole man. That per­sona, he said, may be au­then­tic to him, “but it’s not all that I am”.

~ The dan­ger is that an au­di­ence mis­takes a slice for the whole, and in time the per­son may too. People con­tain mul­ti­tudes, Varma ar­gued, and a per­sona that wins ap­proval can shut out the rest. {003-C01}

quote.text: This per­son sim­ply just know me from the show and that’s my per­sona.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the question at the book launch

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what a doctor told him about overtreatment
stories.head: Paracetamol, and nothing else
body: The doc­tor Lancelot Pinto[[x11]] told Amit Varma that dur­ing COVID a sig­nif­i­cant per­cent­age of the deaths were caused by overtreat­ment. {003-S08}

Patients would go to a doc­tor and in­sist on what the neigh­bour had got, iver­mectin and all. Overtreatment could set off a cy­tokine storm, and its re­sults, Varma said if he re­mem­bered cor­rectly, re­ally started after about a week.
When Varma him­self got COVID, Pinto gave him parac­eta­mol and some­thing to gar­gle with. “And that’s it, noth­ing else,” Varma said.
~ For Varma, it shows the gap be­tween a doctor’s dharma, to do what is best for the pa­tient, and the in­cen­tive to give pa­tients what they want, even when they want the wrong thing. {003-C10}
stories.why: A profession’s duty and its in­cen­tives can pull op­po­site ways. When pa­tients de­mand more medicine, the doc­tor who gives less may be the one keep­ing to his call­ing, as Pinto did with Varma.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on overtreatment during COVID

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why the reforms he worked on fell short
stories.head: Economists who knew too little
body: Amit Varma asked why any gov­ern­ment would give up the tools it uses to ha­rass its en­e­mies. Ajay Shah an­swered with a con­fes­sion.

He had been part of the eco­nomic pol­icy process and helped amend laws in an age when the op­por­tu­nity to do things right was “sky high”. They were not done well, he said, “be­cause of in­tel­lec­tual fail­ures of peo­ple like me”[[x12]]. {003-S06}

Mainline econ­o­mists like him saw the world through the lens of eco­nom­ics[[x13]]. They lacked knowl­edge of law, pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion and checks and bal­ances, and as­sumed civil ser­vants were ba­si­cally good.

~ Only in the last 10 to 20 years, he said, has India come to grips with these prob­lems in a deeper way. {#decades} He stays op­ti­mistic: mo­ments for re­form keep com­ing, and when the knowl­edge is there, it can have an im­pact.
stories.why: Missed re­forms are not al­ways about bad in­ten­tions. Sometimes the knowl­edge is miss­ing when the win­dow opens, so build­ing it in ad­vance is how to be ready for the next one.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 3. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. shelf.title: Classical Liberalism – A Primer
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: People often ask Amit what to read to un­der­stand in­di­vid­ual free­dom and clas­si­cal lib­er­al­ism.

shelf.title: Friedrich Hayek: The Ideas and Influence of the Libertarian Economist
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: Butler’s short primer on Hayek, a friendly way into a thinker whose own books can be heavy going (‘though what a great writer’, Amit adds).

shelf.title: Ludwig von Mises – A Primer
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: A short, clear, free in­tro­duc­tion to Mises from a writer Amit rates highly.

shelf.title: Milton Friedman: A Concise Guide to the Ideas and Influence of the Free-Market Economist
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: A con­cise in­tro­duc­tion to Friedman’s ideas for any­one cu­ri­ous about free-market think­ing.

shelf.title: Public Choice – A Primer
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: A short, mas­ter­ful in­tro­duc­tion to pub­lic choice the­ory, read­able in under an hour, that ex­plains why state fail­ure is prac­ti­cally ev­ery­where though ev­ery­one talks only of mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Adam Smith – A Primer
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: An ac­ces­si­ble entry point to one of the thinkers Amit most often gets asked how to read.

shelf.title: Lifespan: Why We Age – and Why We Don’t Have To
shelf.creator: David Sinclair
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great book on the case that we can live healthy, ac­tive lives past a hun­dred rather than de­cline into decades of de­men­tia.

shelf.title: Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevity
shelf.creator: Peter Attia
shelf.why: More read­ing on the episode’s idea that much longer, health­ier lives are pos­si­ble.

shelf.title: The Nurture Assumption: Why Children Turn Out the Way They Do
shelf.creator: Judith Rich Harris
shelf.why: Amit calls it one of the sem­i­nal so­cial sci­ence books of the last cen­tury.

shelf.title: Reforms of prosecution in the Indian criminal justice system
shelf.creator: Smriti Parsheera
shelf.why: Ajay calls it a very nice ar­ti­cle on the prob­lems of pros­e­cu­tion in India.

shelf.title: FSLRC Report and Draft Indian Financial Code
shelf.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
shelf.why: The FSLRC re­port, a crisp sum­mary of 20 years of Indian re­search on reg­u­la­tion writ­ten as com­pact chap­ters end­ing in draft­ing in­struc­tions, and the draft Indian Financial Code it pro­duced.

shelf.title: Murali Neelakantan Looks at the World (Episode 329, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Murali Neelakantan
shelf.why: This is where Murali ex­plained why per­jury ends a lawyer’s ca­reer in England but is ex­pected in India.

shelf.title: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
shelf.why: Dr Lancelot Pinto, one of the rare doc­tors who reads pa­pers daily, on med­i­cal prac­tice and how overtreat­ment driven by pa­tient de­mand cost lives dur­ing COVID.

shelf.title: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Philips
shelf.why: A long de­fence of sci­en­tific medicine from liver doc­tor Abby Philips, on the ten­sion be­tween doing right by pa­tients and giv­ing them what they want.

shelf.title: Gurwinder Bhogal Examines Human Nature (Episode 331, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Gurwinder Bhogal
shelf.why: The source of the idea that we shape our­selves on the re­flec­tions of us we see in other people’s eyes.

shelf.title: Suyash Rai Embraces India’s Complexity (Episode 307, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
shelf.why: A way into the mind of Suyash Rai, whom Amit re­gards as a great thinker, deeply in­flu­enced by Alasdair MacIntyre, on dharma, India’s com­plex­ity and the lim­its of the state.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
shelf.why: Amit’s adda with friends Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas, the source of sto­ries he keeps re­turn­ing to: the friend who changed his mind about liv­ing long, healthy lives, and tal­ented small-town kids los­ing their depth in Bombay, a re­minder that clus­ters can cor­rupt as well as up­lift.

shelf.title: Avoid hydroponics (anti-recommendation)
shelf.why: Ajay’s anti-recommendation: hy­dro­ponic leaves look clean, but grow­ing plants in water starves their root mi­cro­biome and leaves them nu­tri­tion­ally in­fe­rior, so pre­fer plants grown in healthy soil.

shelf.title: The secret world beneath our feet is mind-blowing – and the key to our planet’s future
shelf.creator: George Monbiot
shelf.why: Background read­ing on the soil life that Ajay ar­gues makes soil-grown food nu­tri­tion­ally su­pe­rior.

shelf.title: Seeing dead fruit flies is bad for the health of fruit flies
shelf.creator: Christi Gendron
shelf.why: The study show­ing that even fruit flies suf­fer shorter lives after see­ing dead fruit flies, ev­i­dence that the mind ‘goes all the way down to flies’.

shelf.title: Beautiful Boy
shelf.creator: John Lennon
shelf.why: The source of the line that cap­tures how life hap­pens to us re­gard­less of our plans.

laughs.text: Ajay ex­plains that he shaved his beard after read­ing Putin’s claim that ev­ery­one sup­ports the in­va­sion of Ukraine ex­cept ‘some bearded intellectuals’. Then he ob­jects: ‘Excuse me, think about Karl Marx, think about Frederick Engels, think about Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, also known as Lenin, think about Leon Trotsky... his pan­theon should be full of bearded in­tel­lec­tu­als. So what has he got against bearded in­tel­lec­tu­als?’
Ajay asks how Amit would be­have if he could fool him­self into think­ing he had 500 years to live. Amit: ‘Dude, the show won’t exist be­cause I pro­cras­ti­nate so much.’
Amit il­lus­trat­ing the look­ing-glass self: around Ajay, ‘I’m gonna cut out the dad jokes and I’m gonna do se­ri­ous econ talk or what­ever I think you want.’
Amit quotes John Lennon, ‘Life is what hap­pens to you when you’re busy mak­ing other plans’, and the come­back fol­lows: ‘Or life is what hap­pens to you while you’re busy mak­ing pod­casts.’
Before chap­ter two, Amit re­ports a producer’s note: ‘My pro­ducer just told me do some­thing about your cleav­age. So I’ve kind of brought my shirt to­gether.’
Ajay on in­sti­tu­tional re­form: ‘Law is too im­por­tant to be left to the lawyers.’
After Ajay’s case against hy­dro­ponic leaves, Amit says: ‘Anybody who’s eat­ing a leaf, it’s a su­per­fi­cial joy only,’ no mat­ter how it is grown.

Amit’s sign-off: ‘Subscribe and like. I for­got to say it in the pre­vi­ous episodes, but if you’re a YouTuber, you’re sup­posed to say that,’ fol­lowed by an apol­ogy for what his pro­ducer calls his ‘rest­ing pout face’.

Amit adds his own bearded hero: ‘Figure num­ber one in my pan­theon, be­cause I’m half Bengali, is Robi-da’ (Rabindranath Tagore), who had a flow­ing beard and, Amit is sure, would not have ap­proved of the war on Ukraine, or of na­tion­al­ism ei­ther.
‘The mukhota be­comes a mukh’: Amit’s Hindi phrase for the mask be­com­ing the face, the episode’s cen­tral warn­ing about per­sonas.
On a journalist’s dharma, Amit cites the old max­ims of speak­ing truth to power and ‘to af­flict the com­fort­able and to com­fort the afflicted’.

Introducing the Butler primers, Amit cites the say­ing ‘if you’re not a com­mu­nist at 18, you don’t have a heart. If you’re not a cap­i­tal­ist at 28, you don’t have a head.’ He ar­gues that the ideas we ab­sorb young feel vir­tu­ous but are often il­lib­eral.
